2400:
Buzzworthy means "interesting or exciting enough to make many people talk about it."

When something is buzzworthy, it grabs people's attention so strongly that they feel the urge to discuss it, share it, recommend it, or comment on it — whether in person, on social media, in news articles, or in group chats.

Think of it this way: "buzz" is the noise that comes from a crowd of excited people all talking at once. A "buzzworthy" thing is something worthy of creating that noise — something so striking, surprising, entertaining, or impressive that it naturally gets people chattering.

Something earns the label "buzzworthy" when it has a quality that makes people feel: "I have to tell someone about this."

That quality could be:

  • Surprising or unexpected — a shocking plot twist in a TV show
  • Impressive or excellent — a movie that blows everyone away
  • New and exciting — a product nobody has seen before
  • Controversial — a celebrity saying something provocative
  • Funny or clever — a commercial so witty that people send it to their friends
  • Culturally relevant — something that perfectly captures the mood of the moment

The key is that the thing generates talk. It doesn't just sit quietly in the world — it spreads, gets shared, gets debated, gets recommended.

"Buzzworthy" is mostly a positive or neutral word, but it can occasionally carry a slightly negative edge, depending on context.

  • Positive use: "Her debut album is genuinely buzzworthy — critics can't stop talking about it." (Here, it means the album is impressive and deserves all the praise it's getting.)
  • Neutral/descriptive use: "The ad campaign was buzzworthy, though people were divided on whether they liked it." (Here, it just means it attracted a lot of attention and discussion — but not necessarily all good.)
  • Slightly negative use: "The film was buzzworthy mostly because of its terrible ending." (Here, the "buzz" is not entirely complimentary — it generated talk, but that talk included criticism.)

So the word focuses more on the amount of attention and talk something receives, rather than making a strict judgment about whether that attention is good or bad. That said, in everyday usage, calling something "buzzworthy" usually leans toward being a compliment or a sign of excitement.

Not everything buzzworthy generates the same intensity of attention. The word can describe:

  • Locally buzzworthy — a new restaurant in your neighbourhood that everyone in your circle is talking about
  • Regionally buzzworthy — a political speech that dominates conversation in a city or state
  • Nationally buzzworthy — a sports moment that the whole country is discussing
  • Globally buzzworthy — a viral video that people everywhere are sharing and reacting to

The word works at all these scales. Context usually makes it clear how wide the buzz is.
Where You'll Commonly See It Used

"Buzzworthy" appears most frequently in:

  • Entertainment journalism — reviews and previews of films, TV shows, albums, and books
  • Marketing and advertising — describing campaigns or products that generated excitement
  • Social media discussions — influencers, commentators, and journalists describing trending topics
  • Tech and business coverage — new gadgets, startup launches, or bold company announcements
  • Pop culture commentary — anything related to fashion, celebrity culture, food trends, or internet moments

Examples in sentences:

  • "The trailer for the new superhero film is easily the most buzzworthy thing on the internet this week."
  • "Brands spend millions trying to create buzzworthy content, but truly viral moments are rarely planned."
  • "Her speech at the conference was buzzworthy — my entire LinkedIn feed was full of quotes from it."
  • "The restaurant's bizarre menu made it buzzworthy, but the food itself was disappointing."
  • "It's a small film with a tiny budget, but the ending is so unexpected that it's become genuinely buzzworthy."
The Difference Between Buzzworthy and Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

  • Popular means many people like or consume something. Buzzworthy means many people are talking about it. You can be popular without being buzzworthy (a classic, beloved old song), and buzzworthy without being universally popular (a controversial art installation).
  • Viral means something has spread very rapidly and widely, especially online. Buzzworthy is broader — it can include things that haven't gone fully viral but are still generating significant conversation. Viral is like the explosive version of buzz.
  • Trendy means something is currently fashionable or in style. Buzzworthy is about conversation and attention, not necessarily fashion. A shocking documentary can be buzzworthy without being "trendy."
  • Noteworthy means deserving of attention because of its significance or quality. Buzzworthy means attention is already happening or is very likely to happen. Noteworthy is more formal; buzzworthy is more about the social energy around something.

If you had to put the word in one sentence, it would be:

Buzzworthy describes something so interesting, exciting, surprising, or impressive that it makes people want to talk about it, share it, or react to it.

It's a word that lives at the intersection of quality and social energy — the idea that something doesn't just sit there being good, it actively stirs up conversation and excitement in the world around it.
2401:
"By all accounts" means according to what everyone says, or according to all the information available. You use it when you are reporting something that you have not personally witnessed or verified yourself, but that many people — or all available sources — seem to agree on.

Think of it as saying: "I wasn't there, and I can't swear to this myself — but from everything I've heard, read, or been told, this is true."

The word "accounts" here doesn't mean bank accounts. It means reports, descriptions, or testimonies — the things people say about an event, a person, or a situation. Think of "account" as in "eyewitness account" or "giving an account of what happened."

So "by all accounts" literally means "going by all the reports/testimonies" — meaning: every source of information points to the same conclusion.
The Core Idea — Why This Idiom Exists

Imagine you never met a famous chef, but your friend, your colleague, a food magazine, and a TV show all say the same thing: he is extraordinarily talented. You haven't tasted his food yourself. But by all accounts, he is a genius in the kitchen.

The idiom exists to signal two things at once:

  1. Agreement across multiple sources — it's not just one person's opinion.
  2. You are not a direct witness — you are passing on a widely shared understanding, not a personal fact.

This makes it an honest, careful phrase. It lets you say something with confidence without overclaiming.
How and Where to Use It

"By all accounts" is almost always placed at the beginning of a sentence or clause, though it can also appear mid-sentence. It works in both spoken and written English, and it suits formal, semi-formal, and everyday conversation.

Examples:

  • By all accounts, the concert was absolutely spectacular.

(Everyone who was there seems to be saying it was spectacular — I wasn't there, but that's the unanimous report.)

  • She had, by all accounts, a very difficult childhood.

(Placed mid-sentence. All sources — biographies, interviews, friends — suggest her childhood was hard.)

  • By all accounts, the new restaurant on Fifth Avenue is worth the wait.

(Every review and every person who's been there seems to agree.)

  • He was, by all accounts, one of the greatest scientists of the 20th century.

(History, biographies, and expert opinions all point to this conclusion.)

  • The journey was, by all accounts, extremely dangerous.

(All who made it, wrote about it, or studied it seem to agree on this.)

Here is the most important thing to understand about this idiom: it signals intellectual honesty.

When you say "by all accounts," you are implicitly admitting:

  • "I don't know this firsthand."
  • "But the evidence — from many people and sources — strongly points this way."

This is different from saying "everyone says" (which sounds gossip-like and informal) or "it is a fact that" (which is a direct claim). "By all accounts" sits elegantly in the middle — it is confident but humble.

This is why journalists, authors, historians, and educated speakers use it often. It is a graceful way to report something broadly agreed upon without pretending to have direct knowledge.

• It does not mean you personally verified the information.
  • It does not mean you are guessing or speculating (that would be "apparently" or "supposedly").
  • It does not require literally every single person to agree — it means the general consensus, the overwhelming weight of reports, points in one direction.
  • It is not a negative or doubtful phrase. It actually leans positive — toward belief and agreement, not skepticism.

Understanding nearby expressions helps you truly master this one.

"Apparently" — suggests something seems to be true, but there is a mild hint of uncertainty or surprise. It can even carry a slightly doubtful tone. "By all accounts" is more confident and rooted in multiple sources.

"Reportedly" — used especially in journalism. It means one or more sources have reported something, but it hasn't been officially confirmed. "By all accounts" implies broader agreement across many sources, not just one or two.

"From what I hear" — informal and personal. It signals you specifically heard something. "By all accounts" sounds more universal and objective.

"By all indications" — nearly the same meaning, but uses evidence and signs rather than human testimony. You might say "by all indications, the economy is recovering" using data, trends, and signs — not just what people are saying.

This idiom has a slightly formal, educated tone to it. It is perfectly natural in everyday speech among adults, but it is not slang. You would not typically hear a child use it. It fits well in:

  • News articles and journalism
  • Books and biographies
  • Academic writing (in moderation)
  • Professional conversation
  • Storytelling and personal essays
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

Suppose you are talking about a historical figure — say, a great general from 200 years ago — whom no living person ever met. You might say:

"By all accounts, she was a brilliant military strategist — fearless in battle, deeply respected by her soldiers, and decades ahead of her time in tactics."

You weren't there. No one alive was. But historians, letters, battle records, and countless accounts all paint the same picture. That is exactly what "by all accounts" is built for.

"By all accounts" means: "Based on everything that has been said or reported by others — even though I haven't witnessed it myself — this appears to be true."

It is a confident, honest, and elegant idiom that shows you are well-informed and careful with your words at the same time.
2402:
"By all means" is a phrase used to say "yes, absolutely" or "of course" — but with warmth, enthusiasm, and zero hesitation. It is a polite, emphatic way of giving someone permission to do something or encouraging them to go ahead with something.

When you say "by all means," you are not just agreeing. You are signaling that the other person should feel completely free, welcome, and comfortable to do what they are asking about.

To truly understand this phrase, it helps to look at the word "means."

Here, "means" is a noun, not a verb. It means a method or a way of doing something. (Think of it like the phrase "a means to an end," where "means" = a method or path.)

So "by all means" literally translates to "by using every possible method" or "in every possible way."

Over time, this literal sense gave birth to the figurative use: if you are doing something by all means, you are doing it wholeheartedly, without any reservation whatsoever. That is exactly the feeling this phrase carries when used in everyday conversation.

Use 1: Giving Permission or Encouragement (Most Common)

This is how you will hear and use the phrase almost every single time. It is a polished, friendly way to say "yes, go ahead" or "please, feel free."

Examples:

"May I borrow your pen?"
"By all means!"

"Could I ask you a question?"
"By all means, go ahead."

"Do you mind if I open the window?"
"By all means, please do."

"Can I take a look at your report?"
"By all means."

In all of these, the speaker is giving permission happily and without any hesitation. There is a sense of generosity and openness in the phrase. It makes the other person feel welcome and not like a burden.

Use 2: "No Matter What / At Any Cost" (Less Common, More Formal)

In a secondary, older use, "by all means" can mean "using every possible method" or "no matter what it takes." This use is more formal and is found more often in writing than in everyday speech.

Examples:

"We must, by all means, prevent this from happening."

(= We must use every possible method to prevent this.)

"The mission must by all means be completed before dawn."

(= The mission must be completed no matter what.)

You are less likely to use this in casual conversation, but it is good to recognize it when you read it.

"By all means" has a formal to semi-formal tone. It is not stiff or cold — it is actually quite warm — but it is more polished than casual expressions like "sure" or "yeah, go ahead."

It signals:

  • Politeness — You are being courteous and respectful.
  • Enthusiasm — You are not reluctantly agreeing; you are genuinely welcoming the request.
  • No hesitation — There is no "um" or "well, I guess so" hidden in it. It is a clean, confident yes.
How It Compares to Similar Phrases

All of the following phrases are in the same family as "by all means," but they carry slightly different weights:

"Of course" — Very close in meaning. Slightly more casual than "by all means." Both are widely used.

"Certainly" — Formal, like "by all means," but feels a little crisper and more businesslike.

"Absolutely" — Enthusiastic and warm, like "by all means," but more casual.

"Sure" — Casual and relaxed. Much less formal than "by all means."

"Please do" — Short, warm, and encouraging, similar in spirit but simpler.

"Feel free" — Friendly and casual. Often used with a follow-up: "Feel free to ask me anything."

Think of it as a spectrum from very casual to very formal:

Sure → Of course → By all means → Certainly

"By all means" sits comfortably toward the formal end, but still feels human and friendly.

This is critical to know, because it is easy to confuse the two.

"By no means" means the exact opposite — "definitely not," "absolutely not," or "not at all."

Examples:

"Is this an easy task?"
"By no means. It will take weeks of hard work."

(= It is definitely not easy.)

"This is by no means the end of the story."

(= This is absolutely not the end of the story.)

So remember:

  • "By all means" = Yes, absolutely, go ahead.
  • "By no means" = No, definitely not.

"By all means" works well in these situations:

  • When someone asks for your permission to do something.
  • When you want to encourage someone to go ahead with something.
  • When you want to sound polite and generous in your agreement.
  • In professional settings, formal conversations, customer service, or writing.

• Avoid it in very casual, relaxed conversations with close friends, where it might sound overly stiff. With friends, "sure," "of course," or "go for it" feels more natural.
  • Do not use it to express your own intentions. It would sound odd to say "I will by all means go to the store" in everyday speech (though the secondary meaning technically allows something like this in formal writing).

A student to a professor: "Professor, may I submit the assignment tomorrow?"
Professor: "By all means. Just make sure it is in by noon."

A guest at a dinner party: "Is it alright if I help myself to some more?"
Host: "By all means! Please, eat as much as you like."

A colleague in a meeting: "Can I share an idea?"
Manager: "By all means, we would love to hear it."

"By all means" = Yes, absolutely — please go right ahead, and do not hesitate for even a second.

It is a polite, warm, and enthusiastic way of saying yes, and once you start noticing it in English conversations and writing, you will see it everywhere.
2403:
"By and large" means "in general" or "on the whole."

You use it when something is mostly true — when you're looking at the big picture and ignoring small exceptions. It's your way of saying: "If I step back and look at everything together, this is what I see."

Think of it like this: imagine you're judging a movie. A few scenes were boring, but most of it was great. You wouldn't say "the movie was perfect" (because it wasn't). But you also wouldn't say "the movie was bad." Instead, you'd say:

"By and large, it was a great movie."

That one phrase does something elegant — it tells the listener that you've considered everything, and your overall conclusion is that it was great.

This is where most learners stop too soon, so pay attention here.

"By and large" does three things at once:

  1. It makes a general statement. You're not talking about one specific case. You're talking about the overall pattern.
  2. It quietly admits exceptions exist. When you say "by and large," you're already signaling that the statement isn't 100% true in every single case. The exceptions are real, but they're small enough that they don't change the big picture.
  3. It shows you've thought it through. It tells your listener that you're making a careful, balanced judgment — not a careless or extreme one.

This is why "by and large" sounds more thoughtful and measured than simply saying "always" or "never." It's the language of someone who considers things fairly.
How to Use It in a Sentence

"By and large" is almost always placed in one of two positions:

At the beginning of a sentence:

By and large, people enjoy being praised for their work.

In the middle, between commas:

The new policy, by and large, has been a success.

Both are correct and natural. Placing it at the beginning gives it a bit more emphasis. Placing it in the middle makes it feel more conversational and woven into the thought.

It is rarely placed at the very end of a sentence, and doing so would sound odd.

Let's look at several examples across different situations so the meaning really sinks in:

By and large, children learn languages faster than adults.

→ This is generally true. There are some adult language-learners who are extraordinarily fast, but they're the exception. The overall pattern favors children.

The construction project was, by and large, completed on time.

→ Maybe one or two sections were delayed, but the overall project was on schedule. The phrase lets the speaker be honest without being misleading.

By and large, the reviews for the restaurant have been positive.

→ Some people may have had a bad experience, but most reviews are good.

Life in a small town is, by and large, quieter than life in a city.

→ Not every small town is quiet, and not every city is loud — but if you look at the general pattern, this statement holds true.

By and large, the students found the exam fair.

→ A few may have complained, but the majority thought it was fair.

Notice the pattern in all these examples: the statement is true overall, even if it's not true in every single case.
What "By and Large" Does NOT Mean

This is important. Many learners confuse "by and large" with words like "always," "definitely," or "completely." It is none of those things.

  • It does not mean every time or always.
  • It does not mean in this specific case.
  • It does not mean perfectly or without exception.

If you say "By and large, he is honest," you are not saying he is perfectly honest in every situation. You're saying: looking at his overall character and behavior, honesty is the general rule.

This is a subtle but very important distinction.
Words and Phrases That Mean the Same Thing

These are all close synonyms. You can often swap them for "by and large" without changing the meaning much:

  • On the whole — On the whole, the event went smoothly.
  • Generally — People generally prefer comfort over style.
  • In general — In general, exercise improves mood.
  • For the most part — For the most part, the feedback was positive.
  • Overall — Overall, it was a good experience.
  • All things considered — All things considered, the plan worked.
  • Broadly speaking — Broadly speaking, the theory is correct.

Each of these carries a slightly different flavor, but they all share the same core idea: this is the general truth, with room for exceptions.

"By and large" is a neutral, slightly formal phrase. It works comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation — "By and large, I enjoy my job."
  • Academic writing — "By and large, the data supports the hypothesis."
  • Journalism and opinion pieces — "By and large, the government's response was inadequate."
  • Business and professional speech — "By and large, our customers are satisfied."

It is not slang. It's not too formal either. It sits comfortably in the middle and sounds educated and thoughtful without being stiff.

"By and large" means generally speaking — you use it to describe what is true in most cases or overall, while quietly acknowledging that small exceptions may exist.

If you can remember that, you've got it. Everything else above just helps you use it with precision and confidence.
2404:
This idiom means "even if you try as hard as possible to believe or imagine something."

It is almost always used in the negative — to say that something is completely, absolutely untrue or impossible, no matter how creatively or generously you think about it.

Think of it this way: it means "not even close" — but said in a more expressive, emphatic way.
Understanding the Logic Behind It (Why Does It Make Sense?)

To truly own an idiom, you need to understand why it means what it means. Here is the logic:

Imagine your imagination is like a rubber band. Normally, a rubber band has a certain size. But you can stretch it — pull it wider — to make it bigger and fit around something larger.

Now, when someone says "by no stretch of the imagination", they mean: even if you stretch your imagination as wide as it can possibly go — even if you push your mind to its absolute limit trying to believe something — it still won't fit. It still isn't true.

So the "stretch" refers to the mental effort of trying to imagine or believe something that is difficult to accept. And the idiom is saying: no amount of that effort will work.
The Two Main Forms You Will Encounter

1. "By no stretch of the imagination" (most common)

This is the most frequently used version. It's a direct, complete negative.

"He is, by no stretch of the imagination, a professional singer."

This means: No matter how hard you try to think of him as a professional singer, you simply cannot. He is not one.

2. "Not by any stretch of the imagination"

This means exactly the same thing. The negative word ("not") just moves to a different position in the sentence.

"This plan is not, by any stretch of the imagination, going to work."

Both forms (#1 and #2) are interchangeable. You can use either one.

3. "By any stretch of the imagination" (in questions and conditionals)

This form is used without a negative word — but it is usually found inside a question or an "if" situation, where the negative idea is still implied.

"Could this be called good cooking by any stretch of the imagination?"

Here, the speaker is asking the question in a way that strongly implies the answer is no. The tone is often sarcastic or disbelieving.

"If this is a success by any stretch of the imagination, I'll be shocked."

Here are clear, realistic examples showing how native speakers actually use this idiom:

  1. "This film was not, by any stretch of the imagination, enjoyable."

(= The film was terrible. Not even close to enjoyable.)

  1. "By no stretch of the imagination did he deserve that award."

(= He absolutely did not deserve it.)

  1. "She is not, by any stretch of the imagination, ready to lead the team."

(= She is completely unprepared. Not even nearly ready.)

  1. "This tiny room could not, by any stretch of the imagination, fit twenty people."

(= It is impossible. It is far too small.)

  1. "By any stretch of the imagination, can you call this a vacation?" (sarcastic)

(= This is so stressful/bad that it cannot be called a vacation at all.)
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom carries a strong sense of emphasis and disbelief. When someone uses it, they are not just saying something is untrue — they are saying it is so far from the truth that it is almost ridiculous to suggest it.

It can be used in two main tones:

  • Sincere / serious: Making a genuine strong point.

"This is not, by any stretch of the imagination, an acceptable standard of work."

  • Sarcastic / humorous: Mocking or joking about something.

"My cat is not, by any stretch of the imagination, a fitness model — but she certainly thinks she is."

A common confusion for learners: this idiom does not mean that something is hard to imagine simply because it is unusual or surprising. It means something is impossible to believe or justify, no matter how hard you try.

❌ Don't confuse it with: "hard to imagine" or "difficult to picture"
✅ The correct sense is: "impossible to honestly call true, even with maximum mental effort"
Where You Will Most Commonly See It

• In formal writing (essays, criticism, journalism)
  • In spoken English when someone wants to make a strong, emphatic point
  • In sarcastic or humorous everyday conversation

It is a relatively formal-to-neutral idiom. It sounds polished and educated when used correctly, and it is perfectly natural in both speech and writing.

These phrases carry a very similar meaning, so learning them together will sharpen your understanding:

  • "Not in the slightest" — She is not qualified, not in the slightest.
  • "Not by a long shot" — That's not enough money, not by a long shot.
  • "Far from it" — Was the food good? Far from it.
  • "In no way" — This is in no way acceptable.
  • "There's no way" — There's no way that counts as art.

All of these mean something is absolutely not the case, just like our idiom — but "by any stretch of the imagination" is richer and more expressive than most of them.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Core meaningEven trying as hard as possible to believe something, it still isn't true
Almost always usedIn the negative
Most common form"By no stretch of the imagination"
ToneEmphatic, strong, sometimes sarcastic
RegisterNeutral to formal; works in speech and writing

Core meaning: Even if you try your absolute hardest to believe something, it is still not true.
Almost always used in the negative.
Most common form: "By no stretch of the imagination."
Tone: Emphatic, strong, sometimes sarcastic or humorous.
Register: Neutral to formal — works naturally in both speaking and writing.
One Final Tip to Remember It Forever

Picture someone physically stretching a rubber band around an object that is simply too big — no matter how hard they pull, the rubber band snaps back. That's exactly what this idiom describes: your imagination stretching and stretching, and still not being able to wrap around an idea because it just isn't true.

That image alone will make this idiom stick with you permanently.
2405:
"By chance" means that something happened without being planned, intended, or expected. It was not arranged. Nobody made it happen on purpose. It simply happened on its own, due to luck, fate, or randomness.

Think of it this way: Imagine you throw a coin in the air. You don't control where it lands — it could be heads or tails. That result happens by chance. Nobody planned it. Nobody caused it deliberately.

The heart of this idiom is this simple contrast:

Planned → On purpose → Intentional
Not planned → By chance → Accidental / Unexpected

When something happens "by chance," it belongs to the second group — it was not in anyone's plan or control.

The word "chance" comes from the Old French word cheance, which itself came from the Latin word cadere, meaning "to fall." In ancient times, people used to roll dice or drop objects to make decisions, and whatever result the dice "fell" into was the result of luck — not choice. Over time, "chance" became the English word for luck, randomness, and unexpected happenings. So, "by chance" literally means "by the way things happened to fall."

"By chance" is a very flexible idiom. It appears in many types of sentences — past events, questions, and even hypothetical situations.

Pattern 1: Describing something that happened unexpectedly

I met my old school friend by chance at the airport.

(You didn't plan to meet them. You didn't know they'd be there. It just happened.)

She found the missing letter by chance while cleaning her desk.

(She wasn't specifically looking for it. She stumbled upon it unexpectedly.)

By chance, he arrived at the exact moment she needed help.

(Perfect timing — but completely unplanned.)

Pattern 2: Asking politely and hesitantly (using "by any chance")

Here, the idiom is often extended to "by any chance", which is used to ask a question in a soft, polite, hopeful way. It shows you're not sure of the answer, but you're hoping it might be yes.

Do you, by any chance, know where the nearest pharmacy is?
Did you, by any chance, see my umbrella?
Are you, by any chance, Dr. Smith's assistant?

This use is very common in polite conversation. It makes the question feel less demanding.

Pattern 3: Emphasising luck or coincidence

By sheer chance, the two scientists were working on the same problem in different countries — and they found the same answer.

The word "sheer" is sometimes added before "chance" to make the meaning even stronger — meaning pure luck, with absolutely no planning whatsoever.
The Feeling and Tone of "By Chance"

"By chance" is generally neutral or positive in tone. It often carries a feeling of surprise or wonder — like something magical or lucky happened without anyone engineering it.

For example:

  • "They met by chance at a café and ended up getting married."

This sounds romantic and serendipitous — a beautiful accident.

Compare this with "by accident," which sometimes has a slightly negative or careless tone:

  • "I deleted the file by accident."

Both "by chance" and "by accident" mean something unplanned happened, but:

  • By chance → Usually neutral or pleasant; a lucky or surprising coincidence.
  • By accident → Can suggest a mistake or an unwanted outcome.

They can sometimes be used interchangeably, but this tonal difference is worth keeping in mind.
Words That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

These expressions carry a very similar meaning to "by chance":

  • Accidentally — "I accidentally found the answer."
  • Coincidentally — "Coincidentally, we were both in London the same week."
  • Unexpectedly — "She unexpectedly ran into her cousin."
  • By coincidence — "By coincidence, they wore the same outfit."
  • By accident — "By accident, he clicked the right button."
  • As luck would have it — "As luck would have it, a taxi appeared just as it started raining."
  • Fortuitously (more formal) — "Fortuitously, the right person called at the right time."

If "by chance" means unplanned, then its opposites are all the expressions that mean planned or deliberate:

  • On purpose — "She did it on purpose."
  • Deliberately — "He deliberately chose that path."
  • Intentionally — "They intentionally arrived early."
  • By design — "By design, the meeting happened at that time."
  • Knowingly — "She knowingly made that choice."

"By chance" works comfortably in both formal and informal situations.

  • Informal (everyday conversation): "I ran into Jake by chance at the gym!"
  • Formal (writing, academic, professional): "The discovery was made by chance during a routine experiment."

This is one reason the idiom is so popular — it fits almost every situation.

Many great discoveries in history happened by chance. The most famous example is penicillin. In 1928, scientist Alexander Fleming wasn't looking for an antibiotic. He accidentally left a petri dish uncovered, and mold (which later became penicillin) grew on it and killed the bacteria around it. He noticed this unexpected result and investigated further. The discovery that saved hundreds of millions of lives happened entirely by chance.

This shows how powerful and real the concept of "by chance" is — not just in language, but in life itself.

MeaningSomething happened without being planned, intended, or expected — due to luck or randomness.
ToneUsually neutral to positive; often carries a sense of surprise or wonder.
Used forDescribing unexpected events, asking polite questions, emphasising coincidence.
Key variation"By any chance" → used in polite, hesitant questions.
SynonymsBy accident, coincidentally, unexpectedly, as luck would have it.
AntonymsOn purpose, deliberately, intentionally, by design.

The beauty of "by chance" is in its simplicity — it captures that universal human experience of life surprising you, of something good or unexpected landing in your lap without you lifting a finger to make it happen.
2406:
1. The Simple Meaning

"By dint of" means "by means of," "through the use of," or "as a result of."

It tells you how something was achieved — what method, effort, force, or quality made something happen.

One-line example:

She became fluent in French by dint of years of daily practice.

Translation: She became fluent because of / through years of daily practice. Her hard work is what made it happen.

That's the core. Everything below will deepen and sharpen your understanding.
2. The Word "Dint" — What Does It Actually Mean?

To truly understand the idiom, you need to understand the word "dint" at its heart.

"Dint" originally meant a blow, a strike, or the dent/mark left by a powerful force. Think of the mark left on a shield after a sword strikes it. That mark is a "dint."

You can still hear this ancient sense in the modern word "dent" — as in a dent in a car. Dint and dent are actually cousins, born from the same root.

So historically, "by dint of" literally meant "by the force of the blow of." Over centuries, this physical, violent sense softened and expanded. The "blow" or "force" became any kind of effort, means, or quality that produces a result. The physical strike became a metaphor for any driving force.

Today, "dint" does not exist as a standalone word in modern English — it only survives in this one frozen phrase: "by dint of." This makes it an idiom, because you cannot use "dint" freely in a sentence on its own.
3. The Full Structure of the Idiom

The phrase always follows this pattern:

By dint of + [noun / noun phrase / gerund (-ing word)]

The thing that comes after "by dint of" is the means — the effort, quality, skill, or method responsible for the outcome.

PartRole
By dint of= "through / because of / by means of"
[noun or -ing word]= the method, effort, or quality that caused the result

The phrase "by dint of" is always followed by a noun or an -ing verb form (gerund). The word or phrase that follows describes what caused or enabled the result.

Examples of what can follow it:

  • By dint of hard work...
  • By dint of persistence...
  • By dint of repeating the same argument...
  • By dint of sheer luck...
  • By dint of his charm and intelligence...

Effort and hard work:

By dint of working sixteen-hour days, the startup finally turned profitable.

= The startup became profitable because of / through sixteen-hour workdays.

Intelligence or skill:

By dint of her brilliance, she solved a problem that had stumped scientists for decades.

= Her brilliance is what made her solve it.

Repetition and persistence:

By dint of asking the same question over and over, the journalist finally got an answer.

= The journalist succeeded through relentless asking.

Luck or chance:

He survived the accident by dint of sheer luck.

= He survived purely because of luck.

Position or status:

By dint of being the CEO's son, he was promoted quickly.

= He was promoted simply because of (or by virtue of) his family connection.

Combination of qualities:

By dint of patience, careful planning, and a bit of good fortune, they completed the expedition.

Notice in all of these, the structure is the same: something happened, and "by dint of" points to what caused or enabled it.
5. The Tone and Register — When Do People Use It?

This is important for a learner.

"By dint of" is formal and somewhat old-fashioned. You will find it far more often in:

  • Written English (books, essays, journalism, formal reports)
  • Literature and academic writing
  • Formal speeches

You will almost never hear it in casual conversation. Nobody at the dinner table says, "I got a taxi by dint of waving my arm." In everyday speech, people say "by means of," "through," "because of," "thanks to," or "using."

So, as a learner, you should:

  • Recognize and understand it when reading formal texts. ✅
  • Use it in formal writing if you want to sound sophisticated and precise. ✅
  • Avoid it in casual speech — it will sound stiff and unnatural. ✅
6. What Makes It Different From Simple Alternatives?

You might ask: "Why not just say 'because of' or 'through'?"

Good question. Here's the nuance:

"By dint of" carries a subtle sense of effort, determination, or force. It implies that the means used was active, sustained, or non-trivial. It often quietly signals that something took real work or a particular quality — that the result didn't come easy.

Compare:

  • "She became successful because of her hard work." — Neutral statement.
  • "She became successful by dint of her hard work." — Has a slightly grander, more emphatic ring. It underscores that the hard work was the driving force, the very thing that made it happen.

That said, the difference is subtle, not dramatic. In most cases, "by dint of" can be replaced by "through," "by means of," or "because of" without losing much meaning. Its main special quality is its formal elegance and its slight emphasis on the active or effortful nature of the means.

These phrases are close in meaning and can often replace "by dint of":

  • By means of — Very similar, slightly more neutral.
  • By virtue of — Often used when the means is a quality, status, or right (by virtue of her experience).
  • Through — Simple and versatile (through hard work).
  • Thanks to — Friendly, often used when the outcome is positive (thanks to your help).
  • On account of — More focused on reason/cause.
  • By force of — Very close to "by dint of," emphasizes power or strong will (by force of habit).
8. How NOT to Use It — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Using "dint" alone
❌ "She succeeded by pure dint."
✅ "Dint" only works inside the fixed phrase "by dint of." You cannot use it freely.

Mistake 2: Confusing "dint" with "dent"
❌ "By dent of hard work..."
✅ The correct spelling in this phrase is always "dint," not "dent" — even though they share a historical root.

Mistake 3: Using it in casual conversation
❌ "I found parking by dint of circling the block three times." (sounds strange in conversation)
✅ Save it for formal writing or elevated prose.

Mistake 4: Putting a verb (not a gerund) after it
❌ "By dint of she worked hard..."
✅ After "by dint of," always use a noun or an -ing form: "by dint of working hard."

Think of the old image of a knight striking a shield. The dint (dent) in the shield was made by the force of the blow.

Now, imagine that "force" or "blow" is any effort, quality, or means. "By dint of" = "by the force of."

By dint of ten years of practice = By the force of ten years of practice.

That mental image will lock it in.

• Meaning: "By means of," "through," or "as a result of." It tells you how something was achieved.
  • Origin: "Dint" = an old word for a blow or strike. The phrase evolved from "by the force of a blow" to "by means of any effort or quality."
  • Structure: By dint of + noun / gerund (-ing form).
  • Tone: Formal, literary, old-fashioned. Not for casual speech.
  • Nuance: Suggests that the means involved real effort, force, or a notable quality.
  • "Dint" today: Only exists inside this phrase. Cannot be used alone.
  • Spelling: Always "dint," never "dent."
  • Closest alternatives: "by means of," "through," "by virtue of."
2407:
"By far" means by a great amount or by a large margin.

You use it to say that something is not just slightly more or better or worse than others — but a lot more, better, or worse. It shows a big, clear gap between one thing and everything else.

Think of it this way:

Imagine a race. If the winner finishes just one second ahead, you would say, "She won." But if she finishes five minutes ahead of everyone else, you would say, "She won by far." That big gap is exactly what "by far" expresses.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

• "Far" = a great distance or degree
  • "By" = indicating how much, or the margin/extent

So "by far" = by a great degree; by a large margin.

It is not a metaphor about physical distance. The word far here is used to describe degree — how much something differs from the rest.
The Golden Rule of Using "By Far"

"By far" is almost always used with:

  1. Superlatives — words like the best, the worst, the most, the least, the greatest, the hardest, etc.
  2. Comparatives — words like better, worse, more, less, faster, cheaper, etc.

This is important. "By far" needs a comparison to work. It is always saying: compared to everything else, this one stands out — by a lot.

With Superlatives (the most common use):

  • This is by far the best pizza I have ever eaten.

(Not just the best — but the best by a huge margin. There is no close second.)

  • Math is by far the hardest subject for me.

(Other subjects are hard too, but math is much, much harder.)

  • He is by far the most talented player on the team.

(The other players are good, but he is in a completely different league.)

  • That was by far the worst film I have seen this year.

(Other bad films exist, but this one was far worse than all of them.)

With Comparatives:

  • This method is by far more efficient than the old one.

(Not just a little more efficient — significantly more efficient.)

  • She speaks English by far better than I do.

(The gap between her English and mine is very large.)
Where Does "By Far" Go in a Sentence?

"By far" is flexible. It can appear in three positions:

1. Before the superlative or comparative (most common):

  • She is by far the strongest candidate.

2. At the end of the sentence:

  • She is the strongest candidate by far.

3. At the beginning of the sentence (less common, more emphatic):

  • By far, she is the strongest candidate.

All three mean exactly the same thing. The position changes only the emphasis and rhythm of the sentence, not the meaning.

When you use "by far," you are not just stating a fact — you are also expressing a sense of "it's not even close."

It carries a tone of certainty and emphasis. It tells the listener: Don't even bother comparing. The gap is huge. There is a clear winner (or loser).

For example:

  • "A is better than B" — simple, neutral comparison.
  • "A is by far better than B" — strong, emphatic, no contest.

To keep things clear, here is what "by far" is not:

  • It does not mean "so far" (which means "up to this point in time").
  • It does not mean "by chance" or "barely."
  • It does not mean "somewhat" or "slightly." In fact, it means the opposite — a large, clear difference, not a small one.

If something is only slightly better, you would not use "by far." You might say "a little better" or "somewhat better" instead.

Here is a simple mental image to lock it in:

Imagine two mountains. One is 1,000 metres tall. The other is 8,000 metres tall. You would say: "The second mountain is by far the taller one." The gap is so obvious, so massive, that there is no debate.

Whenever you use "by far," picture that giant gap between the two mountains.

Core meaningBy a great amount; by a large margin
Used withSuperlatives (the best, the most) and Comparatives (better, more)
What it signalsA big, clear, undeniable gap — not even close
ToneEmphatic, certain, confident
PositionBefore or after the comparison, or at the start of the sentence

And that's everything about "by far" — one of the most commonly used emphasis idioms in both spoken and written English. Once you understand that it simply means "by a great margin," you will start noticing it everywhere.
2408:
"By fits and starts" means doing something irregularly — in short, sudden bursts of activity, followed by stops, pauses, or periods of doing nothing — and then picking it up again, only to stop again. It describes a pattern that is inconsistent, unsteady, and unpredictable, rather than smooth, continuous, or disciplined.

Think of it this way: the opposite of "by fits and starts" is doing something steadily, consistently, and without interruption. If you jog every single day without skipping, that's steady. But if you jog hard for three days, then do nothing for two weeks, then jog once, then disappear again — that's moving forward by fits and starts.

This idiom is built from two old words that most people today don't fully understand.

"Fit" — in modern English, you probably know "fit" as a noun meaning a sudden, uncontrolled episode — like a "fit of laughter," a "fit of rage," or an "epileptic fit." That's exactly the sense here. A fit, in the context of this idiom, means a sudden, brief burst of energy, emotion, or activity. It doesn't last long. It comes on sharply and then disappears.

"Start" — here, "start" does not mean "to begin" in the way we normally use it today. This is the older meaning of "start" — a sudden, brief jerk or movement, like when a loud noise makes you flinch and jump. You've probably said, "That sound made me start" or heard someone say they "started in surprise." That's the word being used here. A start is a quick, involuntary lurch forward — sudden and brief.

So when you put them together — "fits and starts" — you get two words that both mean short, sudden, irregular movements or bursts. The phrase doubles up on the idea to make it vivid and emphatic: sudden burst, sudden burst, sudden burst... with gaps and stillness in between.
A Simple Analogy to Make It Stick

Imagine an old car that keeps breaking down. You turn the key, and the engine roars for a few seconds — then dies. You try again, and it runs for a bit — then sputters and dies again. You try once more, and this time it goes a little longer before cutting out. You eventually make it down the road, but not in one smooth drive. That car moved by fits and starts.

Now apply the same image to a person, a project, a relationship, a country's progress, or any effort at all — and you've understood the idiom perfectly.

This phrase is genuinely old. Both "fit" and "start" were used individually in Old and Middle English to describe sudden, brief movements or episodes. The pairing of the two words became common in English by the 16th and 17th centuries. William Shakespeare, one of the greatest shapers of the English language, used "fits" in a similar sense — for sudden, spasmodic behavior.

The phrase likely became a fixed idiom because both words reinforced the same idea, making the expression feel rhythmic, emphatic, and memorable. English has many idioms built this way — pairs of near-synonyms that strengthen each other, like "bits and pieces," "odds and ends," and "wear and tear."

Over the centuries, the idiom stayed in use while the individual meanings of "fit" (as a sudden burst) and "start" (as a sudden jerk) became less common in everyday speech. Today, people use the phrase without necessarily knowing what "fit" and "start" each meant on their own — but the full idiom is still widely understood.

These examples cover different contexts — personal habits, work, history, and more — so you can see how flexible the phrase is.

Personal habits:
"He has been trying to learn Spanish by fits and starts for three years, but he's never studied consistently enough to become fluent."

Work and projects:
"The novel was written by fits and starts — sometimes she would write five pages in a single morning, and then not touch it for a month."

Historical and social progress:
"Democracy advanced in that country by fits and starts, with periods of reform followed by setbacks and repression."

Physical or mechanical:
"The old printer worked by fits and starts, sometimes functioning fine, then jamming repeatedly for no clear reason."

Personal relationships:
"Their friendship developed by fits and starts — they'd talk every day for a week, then lose touch for months before reconnecting."

Economic or institutional:
"The company's growth happened by fits and starts in its early years, with a few good quarters followed by periods of stagnation."

Notice one thing in all these examples: in every case, the overall process is moving forward, but not smoothly. The thing is getting done — eventually — but in a lurching, inconsistent, stop-and-go way.
The Tone and Feeling of the Phrase

This is important: "by fits and starts" usually carries a mildly negative or critical tone. It implies that the inconsistency is a flaw, a weakness, or at least something worth noting. When you say someone does something "by fits and starts," you are (gently) suggesting they lack discipline, focus, or sustained energy.

It can also be used in a neutral or descriptive way — to simply describe how something happened historically or naturally, with no blame attached to anyone. For example: "Human civilization progressed by fits and starts, not in a straight line." Here, there's no criticism — it's just an accurate description of how history unfolds.

But if you use it about a person's behavior, there's almost always an undertone of: they could be doing better, they're not being consistent, it's not ideal. Keep this tone in mind when using or interpreting the phrase.

Because the phrase sounds unusual, learners sometimes misinterpret it. Let's clear up what it does not mean.

It does not mean "quickly." Moving by fits and starts is not the same as moving fast. In fact, the inconsistency often makes overall progress slow.

It does not mean "enthusiastically." Even if a "fit" of activity sounds energetic, the phrase as a whole is not about enthusiasm — it's about the pattern of activity, which is irregular.

It does not mean "reluctantly" or "unwillingly." The person or thing described might very much want to progress — they're just doing so in an uneven, inconsistent way.

It does not mean "randomly." Randomness is about unpredictability in direction. "By fits and starts" is specifically about the rhythm of effort or progress — on, off, on, off — not about going in random directions.

Knowing similar expressions helps you understand the idiom more precisely by comparison.

"Sporadically" — the closest single-word synonym. "She exercised sporadically" and "she exercised by fits and starts" mean nearly the same thing, though the idiom is more vivid and emphatic.

"On and off" — very similar and very common. "He's been on and off with his diet" captures the same idea in simpler words.

"In spurts" — means in short, sudden bursts, which is similar, but "in spurts" doesn't emphasize the stopping as strongly as "by fits and starts."

"Intermittently" — means with pauses or gaps in between. It's more formal and clinical. "By fits and starts" is more vivid and informal.

"In dribs and drabs" — a related idiom, but this one is more about doing something in small amounts, not necessarily in an irregular rhythm. There's overlap, but they're not identical.

"Erratically" — means in an irregular, unpredictable way. Close, but "erratically" can also imply strange or bizarre behavior, while "by fits and starts" is focused purely on the inconsistent rhythm of activity.

If you want to remember this idiom easily, picture a person doing push-ups. They do five quickly, then collapse and lie there for a while. Then they struggle back up and do three more, then drop again. Then two more, a long rest, and so on. They never find a rhythm. They're getting the push-ups done — eventually — but in the most uneven, stop-and-go way imaginable.

That image — effortful, inconsistent, lurching forward in short bursts — is "by fits and starts." Lock that image in, and you'll never forget the idiom.

"By fits and starts" = doing something in irregular, short bursts of activity with gaps and stops in between — not smoothly, not steadily, but in an inconsistent, on-and-off pattern. It usually implies that this inconsistency is a weakness or a limitation, though it can also be used neutrally to describe how events or processes naturally unfold over time.
2409:
"By hook or by crook" means by any means necessary — whether the method is easy or hard, fair or unfair, conventional or unconventional. When someone says they will do something "by hook or by crook," they are expressing strong determination. They are basically saying, "I will find a way to make this happen, no matter what it takes."

Think of it as the language version of a person rolling up their sleeves, gritting their teeth, and saying, "I don't care how I get there — I WILL get there."

Imagine your favourite band is coming to your city and tickets are almost impossible to get. You say:

"I am going to get a ticket to that concert by hook or by crook."

This means you'll try every possible option — checking online, asking friends, standing in line early, finding resellers, calling the venue — whatever it takes. You are not going to give up easily.

The word "hook" refers to a curved metal tool, and "crook" also refers to a curved or bent tool (like a shepherd's staff, which has a hooked top). The idea behind the phrase is that you will grab what you need with whatever tool comes to hand — you will not be picky about how you get it done.
The Origin — Where Did This Come From?

This is one of the oldest idioms in the English language. Here are the most credible explanations:

The Medieval Firewood Theory (Most Widely Accepted)

In medieval England, ordinary peasants and common people were not allowed to freely cut wood from the forests owned by lords and nobles. However, there was a rule that said they were allowed to collect fallen branches and dead wood using two specific tools — a billhook (a curved cutting blade used for harvesting) and a shepherd's crook (a long staff with a bent, hooked top used to pull down branches).

So "by hook or by crook" originally described the only two legal ways a poor person could gather wood — by pulling branches down with a hook or dragging them with a crook. Over time, the phrase evolved to mean "by whatever means are available to you."

This theory is considered the most historically plausible because it explains why both tools are mentioned together — they were a real, paired set of tools with a specific legal context.

The Written Record

The phrase is very old. It appears in texts from as far back as the late 1300s — for example, in the writings of John Wycliffe (around 1380) and the poet John Gower (around 1390). This makes it over 600 years old, which confirms it is one of the most enduring idioms in English.

The Cromwell Theory (Popular but Likely a Myth)

A well-known but largely rejected theory claims the phrase comes from Oliver Cromwell, who reportedly said he would capture the Irish city of Waterford "by Hook or by Crooke" — referring to two geographic locations: Hook Head (a peninsula) and Crooke (a village), which were the two possible entry routes into the harbour.

However, since the phrase already appeared in writing before Cromwell was born, most language historians consider this a colourful coincidence, not the true origin. It is what linguists call a folk etymology — a story that sounds convincing but doesn't hold up historically.

The idiom carries a sense of stubbornness, grit, and fierce determination. It often suggests that the person is willing to use unconventional or even slightly questionable methods if necessary — but it does not necessarily mean illegal or criminal actions. It sits somewhere between "I'll work hard for it" and "I'll bend the rules if I have to."

For example:

  • A student saying "I'll pass this exam by hook or by crook" means they'll study all night, find extra resources, ask every teacher — whatever it takes.
  • A businessperson saying "We'll meet this deadline by hook or by crook" means the team will work overtime, find workarounds, bring in extra help — any solution that works.

The phrase does not judge how you succeed. It just emphasises that you will succeed.

Sentence 1:

"The lawyer promised her client that she would win the case by hook or by crook."

(She will use every legal strategy, loophole, and argument she can find.)

Sentence 2:

"After losing his passport abroad, he was determined to get home by hook or by crook."

(He would visit embassies, borrow money, call contacts — anything to get back.)

Sentence 3:

"The company needed to launch the product by Friday by hook or by crook."

(They would work through the night, skip steps, hire extra hands — whatever was needed.)

Sentence 4:

"She raised three children alone and, by hook or by crook, made sure they all went to university."

(She sacrificed, hustled, and found a way through sheer willpower.)

This idiom is informal but widely understood across all English-speaking countries — the UK, USA, Australia, Ireland, and beyond. You can use it in:

  • Everyday conversation — very natural and common.
  • Informal writing — blogs, emails to friends, casual articles.
  • Storytelling and fiction — it adds colour and personality to dialogue.

You would avoid it in very formal writing like a legal document, a scientific paper, or a formal business report — in those contexts, just say "by any means necessary" or "through all available options."

These idioms carry a similar meaning and can sometimes be used in place of "by hook or by crook":

  • "By any means necessary" — direct and strong; slightly more serious in tone.
  • "Come hell or high water" — means "no matter what obstacles appear," with a dramatic flair.
  • "At all costs" — means regardless of the sacrifice involved.
  • "Whatever it takes" — modern, casual, and very commonly used today.

MeaningBy any means necessary; using every possible method to achieve something
ToneDetermined, stubborn, resourceful — sometimes with a hint of rule-bending
RegisterInformal; suitable for conversation and casual writing
AgeOver 600 years old — one of the oldest idioms in English
OriginMost likely from medieval peasants collecting firewood with hooks and crooks
The One-Line Definition to Remember Forever

"By hook or by crook" = "I will succeed using any method available to me, no matter how difficult or unconventional — I simply will not fail."

That's the heart of it. Anytime you feel absolute, stubborn, won't-take-no-for-an-answer determination — that's "by hook or by crook."
